newsitem.title: CANADA: Balanced Canada budget within 2 years - Chretien.
newsitem.headline: Balanced Canada budget within 2 years - Chretien.

text.p: Canada's Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Thursday that he expected his government to balance the budget within two years.
"We'll have a zero deficit with the briefest delay," Chretien told reporters after a retreat with his new cabinet.
"We will maintain our course of having no deficit within two years," he said. "We do think we will balance the books in two years."
He added, however, that he was concerned about high unemployment, especially among youth, and child poverty.
Chretien said he expected job creation to pick up and the Canadian economy to reap the dividends of economic progress made in the past few years.

Some members of Chretien's Liberal caucus have called for the government to move left fiscally, following the loss of two-thirds of the Liberal seats in economically depressed Atlantic Canada in the June 2 election.

Asked if the government was veering left, Chretien said: "This government is not veering left or right. It's moving forward. Sometimes you have curves to the left, sometimes curves to the right, but you're always moving forward."
Chretien said the cabinet had discussed the fiscal situation, unemployment especially among youth, native affairs, modernizing medicare, and national unity.

But he said no new initiatives were discussed. He said further news would have to wait until the inauguration of the new Parliament in September, when government policy would be laid out in a speech from the throne.
The new secretary of state for children and youth, Ethel Blondin-Andrew, repeated on Thursday a Liberal promise to double an C$850 million tax credit for families with children.

Chretien, asked when this would be implemented, showed no sign of rushing into it, noting that the original tax credit was only announced in February and some of it will come into effect only next year.
"We said we would like to double it when we have the means...when we will be in good shape to do it," he said. "As they say, Rome was not built in one day."

Neither he nor his finance minister, Paul Martin, made any direct mention of broad-based tax cuts or of debt reduction, though Chretien pledged in the campaign to devote half of any surplus to new spending and half to cuts in taxes and debt.
Referring to the cabinet meeting, he reported: "We discussed the fiscal situation and determined that we must continue to pursue our objective of a zero deficit with the briefest delay."
